title: High-frequency nonlinear conductivity of a Wigner crystal
authors: A. J. Schleusner, M. T. Elewa, N. R. Beysengulov, C. A. Mikolas, J. Pollanen
abstract: Electrons trapped above the surface of superfluid helium are a disorder-free platform for investigating the formation and dynamics of low-dimensional Wigner crystals. A characteristic nonlinear transport feature of this electronic solid suspended above the helium surface is the Bragg-Cherenkov effect, in which the mobility of the smoothly moving crystal is limited by the coherent emission of helium surface waves (ripplons). The effect has been understood in the conventional Cherenkov setting in which the crystal moves at a constant speed. Here we report on transport measurements of electrons on helium confined in a microchannel geometry to investigate the non-equilibrium response of the Wigner solid when it is subjected to a high-frequency driving field. Surprisingly, the experiments reveal a strongly nonlinear transport response of the confined Wigner solid at frequencies nearly an order of magnitude larger than the ripplon frequencies contributing to the conventional Bragg-Cherenkov effect. We relate this observation to the coupling of the Wigner solid to ripplons with higher-order Bragg vectors, which gives rise to a dynamical friction that provides a mechanism for the observed high-frequency pinning.
summary: The research measures the electrical conductivity of a Wigner crystal on helium at very high frequencies. It finds that the electron solid exhibits nonlinear pinning due to coupling with higher-order ripplon overtones, extending beyond the standard low-frequency Cherenkov mechanism. This demonstrates how collective excitations mediate transport dynamics in strongly correlated quantum systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the high-frequency nonlinear conductivity of a Wigner crystal formed by electrons on superfluid helium.
main_result: The experiment reveals strong nonlinear transport response at frequencies much higher than conventional Bragg-Cherenkov effects, attributed to coupling with ripplon overtones via higher-order Bragg vectors.
method: Transport measurements are performed in a microchannel geometry using AC driving fields and phase-sensitive lock-in techniques, supplemented by an interferometric compensation line to suppress background noise.
model_or_system: The system is a low-dimensional Wigner solid (electron crystal) suspended above superfluid helium. Its dynamics are governed by the interaction between the electrons and the ripplon surface waves.
key_observables: Transport voltage ($V_s$) as a function of driving field amplitude ($V_{ac}$) and bias voltages, showing transitions between liquid and solid states.
important_parameters: High-frequency driving fields (up to 150 MHz), ripplon frequencies ($\omega_{G1}/2\pi \simeq 10$ MHz), and the ratio of Coulomb interaction energy to kinetic energy.
main_assumptions: The conventional Bragg-Cherenkov effect is treated in a quasi-static limit, but the high-frequency analysis extends this by considering higher-order Bragg vectors. The measurement relies on successful background signal cancellation via interference.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images of the device setup, schematics of electrode biasing, and $V_s$ vs. $V_{ac}$ curves demonstrating conductivity transitions at various frequencies (e.g., 0.3 MHz to 150 MHz).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system and low-frequency background theory (Bragg-Cherenkov), details the high-frequency experimental setup including noise mitigation, presents measurements across a wide frequency range, and concludes by interpreting the high-frequency response via higher-order coupling mechanisms.
why_interesting: This work explores non-equilibrium dynamics in an interacting electron solid driven far from equilibrium, providing insights into dynamical friction and phase transitions (melting) mediated by bosonic excitations (ripplons), which is relevant to open quantum systems modeling.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) A false-color scanning electron microscope im- age of the device showing the central electron confining mi- crochannel (red) and electron reservoir (blue) regions. (b) Schematic of the electron system, electrodes, and voltages used to control the electron density and conduct trans- port measurements. (c) Electron transport as a func- tion of the driving field amplitude Vac at a frequency of 300 kHz for increasing central channel bias voltages (Vch = 0.9, 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 V). Inset: Transport signal as a function of Vch for Vac = 150 mV. The transport regimes correspond to an empty channel (I), a high conductivity electron state (II), and a low-conductivity Wigner crystal (III).

FIG. 2. (a) Schematic of the compensation line approach employed to measure the high frequency transport of the microchannel-confined electron system. A voltage tunable attenuator and phase shifter are used to interferometrically reduce the parasitic crosstalk inherent to the device geome- try. (b) The induced transport voltage Vs as a function of the central microchannel bias Vch and the ac driving voltage Vac for f = 0.3, 25, 150 MHz driving fields. The blue, gold, green, and red vertical lines in the top plot correspond to the line-cuts shown in Fig. 1c.

FIG. 3. Velocity of a Wigner solid moving along the cen- tral microchannel. For these data, the electron density in the channel is 7.1 × 109/cm2. Inset: Velocity of the Wigner solid as a function of the driving voltage amplitude at a frequency of 150 MHz. The data trace shows the saturated velocity re- sponse when the electrons in the microchannel are crystallized as well as a sharp transition to a non-equilibrium state of the electron system that moves at a higher velocity.

FIG. 4. The experimentally measured parasitic background for Vac = 0.2 V both with (yellow) and without (blue) com- pensation for the parasitic background signal. The dots are associated with the transport measurements described in the main text while the solid line corresponds to a characteri- zation of the entire background signal when the channel is devoid of electrons. Inset: Ratio of the uncompensated-to- compensated background signal, VUC/VC, as a function of drive frequency, showing an approximately tenfold decrease in the parasitic background.
